spans.content: Global Technology: Accelerating LEO satellite launches; installed base to reach 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E; blue sky at 396k by 2031E

Since launching our global Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite industry estimates in Feb 2025, we have seen accelerated LEO satellite launches in 2025, with LEO satellite installed base at 10k units by 2025 (vs. our previous estimate of 9.7k). We expect this growth momentum to be sustained, supporting a global LEO satellite installed base of 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E in our updated base case. Global satellite operators (e.g., Amazon LEO, Guowang, etc.) are actively updating their satellite launch plans, and expanding satellite applications, including in-flight communication and space data centers, to support commercialization. In this report, we present a blue sky scenario with an installed base reaching 27k/396k units by 2028E/31E, assuming 200k satellite applications made by Chinese vendors (news link) which have seen intensified competition to secure LEO capacity. Read more: Space X Initiation.

Global LEO satellite installed base: 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E

Following the acceleration in LEO satellite launches in 2025, we expect to see continuous growth of satellite installed base from 10k units in 2025 to 13k/17k units by 2026/27E (vs. our last estimate of 12k/15k units by 2026E/27E). We then project the installed base to reach 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E (vs. our previous estimate of 19k/42k units by 2028E/31E), as more operators start or accelerate their launches to secure ideal altitudes in LEO orbit, and as satellite applications expand for commercial use (e.g., space data centers, in-flight communication, emergency communication, autonomous surface vehicles, smart marine ranching, unmanned industrial robots, etc.).

Global satellite operators have updated their satellite plans for LEO orbit, and increased target volumes. Among operators' filings, Amazon LEO received approval from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to launch 4,500 additional LEO satellites (link) in February 2026. Chinese satellite operators submitted applications to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) to seek approval for 200k+ medium- and low-Earth orbit satellites (link).
Exhibit 1: We expect the LEO satellite installed base to reach 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E

Rockets are the key to improving launch pace. (1) Accelerating launch frequency can be effective for the faster growth of satellite launches: in 2025, leading LEO satellite operator Starlink launched satellites every three days; in April 2026, leading rocket supplier SpaceX managed to launch two rockets in 19 hours, implying that there is still room to improve efficiency. (2) Improving rocket capacity: Current mainstream reusable rockets can carry a 17,500 kg payload to LEO, while the next-generation rockets can carry up to 100-150 tonnes. (3) Reusable technology is a milestone: For Chinese LEO satellites, we expect a more rapid ramp-up after the successful development of their domestic reusable rockets.

Blue-sky scenario

We present a blue-sky scenario for the global LEO satellite installed base, which sees the installed base reaching 27k/396k units by 2028E/31E (vs. our base case of 24k/305k units by 2028E/31E), considering the potential for better-than-expected launch capacity of rockets, faster-than-expected monetization of satellite communications, the long-term goals of LEO satellite operators, and the potential upside from space data centers.

In our blue sky scenario, the major upside comes from China LEO satellites, which we do not include in our base case. While technological feasibility remains to be verified, we see strong potential for space data centers given their unlimited access to low-cost solar power supply and their edge-computing capacity, which can handle satellite data directly. Our blue sky scenario is based on the assumption that the 200K LEO constellation plan submitted by Chinese vendors will be achieved in the long-term to reflect the potential for faster commercialization.

China's progress

Accelerating installed base: We expect LEO satellites operated by Chinese vendors to achieve an installed base of 1.9k by 2028E and 24k by 2031E in our base case. In our blue sky scenario, the installed base reaches 101k by 2031E. By end-2025, Chinese vendors were operating 253 units of satellites, marking a deployment ramp-up.
Exhibit 4: Operating satellites of GW and G60 (Jan-24 to Apr-26 Actual)
Data as of April 2026
Source: Company data

Leading vendors have already laid out deployment plans: Key Chinese LEO constellations include GW (Guowang), G60 (or SpaceSail) and Honghu, all of which are large-scale communication constellations that will launch over 10,000 satellites. The GW constellation submitted plans for 12,992 satellites to the ITU in 2020 (per Xinhuanet, link), of which 10% or 1,299 units will need to be launched by 2029. G60 has planned for 15,000 units of satellites, with the goal of reaching 1,296 units by end-2027 and 15,000 units by 2030 (per Xinhuanet, link). Honghu also submitted a plan for 10,000 units of LEO satellites to the ITU in 2024 (per Sina, link), implying that 1,000 satellites need to be in operation by end-2033. Apart from these plans, Chinese satellite operators collectively submitted applications for 200k satellites to the ITU by end-2025 (link), which we view as a strategic move to secure spectrum and orbit resources.

Rockets in fast development: Chinese LEO operators now mainly use LM-6A and LM-12 rockets by China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which are non-reusable. However, development of reusable rockets is accelerating, with more scheduled test flights in 2026. In February 2026, the LM-10 by CASC successfully achieved a first-stage soft-landing splashdown in the sea (link). The Zhuque-3 rocket by LandSpace achieved partial success in a test flight in December 2025, and another recovery test flight will be conducted in 2Q26 (per CCTV, link). The Hyperbola-3 reusable rocket by i-Space will conduct its first launch by end-2026 (per hket, link). The PALLAS-1 reusable rocket by Galactic Energy will also conduct its first launch in 2026 (per futurephecd.com, link).

GS Factor Profile

The GS Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows:

Growth is based on a stock's forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock's forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock's forward-looking P/E, P/B, price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile).

Financial Returns and Multiple use the GS analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).
